tips.title: Outside the bracket does what it says
tips.body: A change written **outside** $f(x)$ affects $y$, and does exactly what you expect: $f(x) + 3$ moves the graph **up** $3$, and $-f(x)$ flips it **through the $x$ axis**. Outside is honest. It is inside the bracket that plays tricks.

tips.title: Inside the bracket goes the opposite way
tips.body: $f(x - 3)$ moves the graph **right** $3$, not left. The reason: to get the same $y$ value you now need an $x$ that is $3$ larger, so every point slides right. Whenever you see a change inside the bracket, expect the opposite sign.

tips.title: Track one point instead of the whole curve
tips.body: You do not need to redraw a curve to answer these. Take a point you know — the turning point, or a root — apply the rule to it, and the rest follows. $(4, 3)$ on $y = f(x)$ becomes $(7, 3)$ on $y = f(x - 3)$ and $(4, -3)$ on $y = -f(x)$.

tips.title: Check with the turning point
tips.body: After sketching, look at where the turning point ended up and ask whether the rule says that. $f(x) + 2$ must lift it by exactly $2$ with its $x$ unchanged; $f(-x)$ must keep its height and flip its $x$. If the turning point is wrong, the whole sketch is.

why.matters:
Once you know one curve you know a family of them. $f(x) + a$, $f(x + a)$, $-f(x)$ and $f(-x)$ are the same shape moved or flipped, so $y = (x - 3)^2 + 2$ can be sketched from $y = x^2$ without a single calculated point.

The reason it is worth more than a sketching trick is that real formulas are usually a standard shape with an offset attached — a starting value, a delay, a reference point. Reading which number does which tells you what the formula is saying, and tells you that changing it moves the picture without changing its shape.

examples.title: What noise-cancelling headphones actually do
examples.body:
A microphone on the outside of the earcup measures the noise arriving as a wave. The headphone then plays **the reflection of that wave in the x-axis** — $-f(x)$ — into your ear. Where the noise pushes, the played sound pulls by the same amount, and the two add to nothing.

It has to be $-f(x)$ and not something merely quiet, because a quieter copy of the noise is still noise. And the timing has to be right to a fraction of a cycle: get it half a cycle late on a 100 Hz drone — 5 thousandths of a second — and the reflection is back in step with the noise, so instead of cancelling it you **double** it.

That is also why it works far better on the steady hum of an engine than on speech. A drone repeats, so the next cycle is predictable and the reflection can be ready in time; a voice does not.

visual.alt: Two sine waves that are reflections of each other in the horizontal axis, the outside noise and the sound the headphone plays, which add to nothing at every point

examples.title: Why a tide table gives one number for a whole harbour
examples.body:
A tide table prints a full day of times for a handful of **standard ports** and then gives every other harbour as a single offset — "high water Port A is 35 minutes after the standard port". One number, not another table.

That works because the tide at a nearby harbour is the same curve horizontally translated: $f(t + a)$. If high water at the standard port is 07:12, then Port A is at 07:47 and Port B, which is 48 minutes **before**, is at 06:24.

And the offset holds for the next tide too: the standard port's next high water is 19:37, so Port A's is 20:12. A translation shifts the whole curve, not one point on it, which is exactly the property that lets the book be thin.

visual.alt: A table of high water times at a standard port and two harbours given as offsets from it, the same offset applying to the morning and the evening tide

examples.title: The same hill, two heights
examples.body:
A hill is 520 m on the map and the village at its foot is 180 m. Ask a walker how high the hill is and you may well be told 340 m, because they are measuring from the valley floor rather than from the sea.

Neither is wrong. Both are the same profile with a different zero, which is $f(x) - 180$: a vertical translation. Every height drops by the same amount, so every **difference** survives untouched — the climb is still 340 m, every gradient is unchanged, and a contour map drawn from either set of numbers has the contours in exactly the same places.

That is the useful half of the idea. A vertical translation changes what the numbers are and nothing about the shape, so it is safe to move the zero to wherever makes the arithmetic easiest — which is why heights on British maps are all measured from one agreed sea level rather than from wherever the surveyor was standing.

visual.alt: Two identical hill profiles drawn one above the other, the same shape measured from sea level and from the valley floor, showing that a vertical shift changes every height and no difference

steps.title: Inside the bracket, or outside it
steps.body:
A transformation takes a graph you already have and moves or flips it. There are four to know, and the whole topic turns on one question:

> Is the change written **inside** the bracket, or **outside** it?

**Outside the bracket is honest.** It affects $y$, and it does what it looks like it does.

- $y = f(x) + a$ moves the graph **up** by $a$.
- $y = -f(x)$ reflects it **in the $x$ axis**, because every $y$ value changes sign.

**Inside the bracket is the opposite.** It affects $x$, and the direction is reversed.

- $y = f(x + a)$ moves the graph **left** by $a$.
- $y = f(-x)$ reflects it **in the $y$ axis**.

**Why inside reverses.** Think about $y = f(x - 3)$. To get the height that $f$ gave at $x = 1$, you now have to put in $x = 4$, because $4 - 3 = 1$. Every height has moved to an $x$ three larger, so the whole graph has slid **right**.

Throughout this topic the example is $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$. Its roots are at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$, its turning point is $(2, -1)$, and it crosses the $y$ axis at $(0, 3)$.

visuals.alt: The curve y equals x squared minus 4x plus 3, with roots marked at 1 and 3 and its turning point marked at 2 comma minus 1

check.solution: The change is outside the bracket, so only the height moves: up by $2$. The turning point goes from $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$.

steps.title: The two reflections
steps.body:
**$y = -f(x)$ reflects in the $x$ axis.** The minus is outside, so every $y$ value changes sign while every $x$ stays where it is. A curve that opened upwards now opens downwards, and a minimum becomes a maximum.

For $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$, the reflection is $-x^2 + 4x - 3$. The turning point moves from $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$ — same $x$, height flipped — and the roots at $1$ and $3$ **stay exactly where they are**, because a point on the $x$ axis has $y = 0$, and $-0 = 0$.

**$y = f(-x)$ reflects in the $y$ axis.** The minus is inside, so every $x$ changes sign while every $y$ stays. For our curve, $f(-x) = x^2 + 4x + 3$: the turning point moves from $(2, -1)$ to $(-2, -1)$, and the roots move from $1$ and $3$ to $-1$ and $-3$.

> $-f(x)$ flips it **vertically**. $f(-x)$ flips it **horizontally**.

**A warning about testing these.** If you try them on $y = x^2$, then $f(-x) = (-x)^2 = x^2$ — the graph does not change at all, because it is already symmetrical about the $y$ axis. That tells you nothing about whether you applied the rule correctly. Always test on a curve that is **not** symmetrical about the $y$ axis, which is why every example here is.

steps.title: Describing a transformation fully
steps.body:
The other half of this topic is the reverse: you are shown two graphs and asked what was done.

**A description has to be complete**, and marks are lost for leaving part of it out.

- For a **translation**: name it, and give the direction and distance. "Translation $3$ to the right" is fine, and so is "translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$". "It moves right" is not — no distance. "Translation by $3$" is not — no direction.
- For a **reflection**: name it, and give the **line**. "Reflection in the $x$ axis". "It is reflected" is not enough.

**Working out which one it was.** Compare a feature you can find on both graphs — the turning point is ideal.

- Same $x$, different $y$: a vertical translation, or a reflection in the $x$ axis if the shape has also turned over.
- Same $y$, different $x$: a horizontal translation, or a reflection in the $y$ axis.
- Turning point unmoved but the curve flipped: look at the roots to tell the two reflections apart.

**And read the equation carefully.** $y = f(x + 4)$ is a move **left** $4$, because $x + 4$ is the same as $x - (-4)$, and the inside rule reverses the sign it finds.

steps.title: Your turn
steps.body:
Throughout, $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$. Its turning point is $(2, -1)$ and its roots are $x = 1$ and $x = 3$.

**Part A — the turning point.**

1. Where is the turning point of $y = f(x) + 2$?
2. Where is the turning point of $y = f(x - 3)$?
3. Where is the turning point of $y = -f(x)$?
4. Where is the turning point of $y = f(-x)$?

**Part B — points and roots.**

5. The point $(4, 3)$ is on $y = f(x)$. Where is it on $y = f(-x)$?
6. Where are the roots of $y = f(-x)$?

**Part C — the ones worth thinking hardest about.**

7. Explain why $y = f(x) + 2$ has no roots at all.
8. A graph is translated so that its turning point moves from $(2, -1)$ to $(-1, -1)$. Write the new equation in the form $y = f(x + a)$ or $y = f(x - a)$.

For question 8, decide which direction it moved before you decide the sign.

props.title: Answer the middle column first, every time

check.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is $(2, -1)$. A translation moves it to $(-1, -1)$. What is the new equation?
check.solution: The height is unchanged and the $x$ has gone from $2$ to $-1$, so it has moved **left** by $3$. A move left is written with a **plus** inside the bracket, so the equation is $y = f(x + 3)$.

steps.title: Going deeper: combining two, and reading one off a sketch
steps.body:
**Two transformations at once.** $y = -f(x) + 4$ has a change inside neither bracket, so both are vertical, and they apply in order: reflect in the $x$ axis first, then move up $4$.

Starting from the turning point $(2, -1)$:

- $-f(x)$ takes it to $(2, 1)$,
- then $+4$ takes it to $(2, 5)$.

The order matters when one of the two is a reflection. Doing $+4$ first would give $(2, 3)$, and then reflecting would give $(2, -3)$ — a different answer entirely. **Work from the inside of the expression outwards.**

**When the transformation is horizontal and vertical**, as in $y = f(x - 3) + 2$, the order does not matter, because the two act on different coordinates: $(2, -1) \to (5, 1)$ either way.

**Reading a transformation off a sketch.** Pick the feature that is easiest to locate on both curves and compare it. Turning points are best; roots are next.

| What moved | What it tells you |
| --- | --- |
| only the height of the turning point | vertical: $f(x) + a$, or $-f(x)$ if the curve also turned over |
| only the $x$ of the turning point | horizontal: $f(x \pm a)$ |
| the curve turned over, roots unmoved | reflection in the $x$ axis |
| the curve the same way up, roots mirrored about $0$ | reflection in the $y$ axis |

**The trap.** A sketch of $y = x^2$ and $y = x^2$ reflected in the $y$ axis looks like one curve, because $x^2$ is symmetrical about the $y$ axis. Exam questions therefore always use an asymmetric curve — and if you are testing your own understanding at home, you should too.

visuals.alt: The curve y equals f of x with the curve y equals minus f of x plus 4, showing the turning point moving from 2 comma minus 1 to 2 comma 5 after a reflection and then a translation

check.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is $(2, -1)$. Where is the turning point of $y = -f(x) + 4$?
check.solution: Work from the inside out. The reflection $-f(x)$ takes $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$, and then $+4$ lifts it to $(2, 5)$. Doing the $+4$ first would give $(2, -3)$, which is why the order matters when a reflection is involved.

steps.title: Summary
steps.body:
- Ask one question first: is the change **inside** the bracket or **outside** it?
- **Outside** affects $y$ and does what it says. **Inside** affects $x$ and reverses.
- $y = f(x) + a$: **up** $a$. $y = f(x) - a$: **down** $a$.
- $y = f(x + a)$: **left** $a$. $y = f(x - a)$: **right** $a$.
- $y = -f(x)$: reflection in the **$x$ axis**.
- $y = f(-x)$: reflection in the **$y$ axis**.
- A point $(a, b)$ moves to $(a, b + 3)$, $(a + 3, b)$, $(a, -b)$ or $(-a, b)$. **Only one coordinate ever changes.**
- Track the **turning point**, not the whole curve.
- $-f(x)$ leaves the **roots** where they are, because $-0 = 0$.
- Describe a **translation** with a direction and a distance; describe a **reflection** with the line.
- Two vertical changes apply **inside out**: reflect before you translate.
- Never test a rule on $y = x^2$; it is unchanged by $f(-x)$ and will tell you nothing.

rows: direction and distance, or the line

questions.prompt: What does the graph of $y = f(x) + 4$ look like, compared with $y = f(x)$?
questions.solution: The change is outside the bracket, so it affects $y$ and does what it says: every point moves **up** by $4$.

questions.prompt: What does the graph of $y = f(x + 4)$ look like, compared with $y = f(x)$?
questions.solution: The change is inside the bracket, so it affects $x$ and reverses: a **plus** inside moves the graph **left**. Reading it as $x - (-4)$ makes the reversal easier to see.

questions.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is at $(2, -1)$. Give the coordinates of the turning point of $y = f(x) + 2$.
questions.solution: Outside the bracket, so only the height changes: up $2$, from $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$.

questions.prompt: In which line is $y = -f(x)$ a reflection of $y = f(x)$?
questions.solution: The minus is outside the bracket, so it acts on $y$: every height changes sign while every $x$ stays. That is a reflection in the **$x$ axis**.

questions.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is $(2, -1)$. Where is the turning point of $y = f(x - 3)$?
questions.solution: Inside the bracket, so only $x$ changes and it moves **right** by $3$: $(2 + 3, -1) = (5, -1)$. The height is untouched.

questions.prompt: The roots of $y = f(x)$ are $x = 1$ and $x = 3$. What are the roots of $y = f(-x)$?
questions.solution: A reflection in the $y$ axis changes the sign of every $x$ coordinate, so the roots move from $1$ and $3$ to $-1$ and $-3$. Their heights are all zero either way.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 3)$ lies on $y = f(x)$. Give the coordinates of the corresponding point on $y = -f(x)$.
questions.solution: The minus is outside, so the height flips and $x$ stays: $(4, 3)$ becomes $(4, -3)$.

questions.prompt: The roots of $y = f(x)$ are $x = 1$ and $x = 3$. What are the roots of $y = -f(x)$?
questions.solution: A root is a point where $y = 0$, and $-0 = 0$, so a reflection in the $x$ axis leaves every root exactly where it was. Only the curve between them turns over.

questions.prompt: Which is a complete description of the transformation from $y = f(x)$ to $y = f(x) - 5$?
questions.solution: A translation needs a direction **and** a distance. "Translation $5$ down" gives both, and the vector form would too. "Translation by $5$" has no direction and "it moves down" has no distance.

questions.prompt: Why does $y = f(x) + 2$ have no roots, when $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$ has two?
options: A translation always removes the roots
Its lowest point is now above the $x$ axis
The curve has turned upside down
Its roots have moved off the visible part
questions.solution: The turning point moves from $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$. The curve opens upwards, so $1$ is the lowest value it ever takes, and that is above the $x$ axis. It therefore never crosses it.

questions.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is $(2, -1)$. Where is the turning point of $y = f(-x)$?
questions.solution: The minus is inside the bracket, so it acts on $x$ alone: the $x$ coordinate changes sign and the height stays. $(2, -1)$ becomes $(-2, -1)$.

questions.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is at $(2, -1)$. A translation moves it to $(-1, -1)$. Write the new equation in the form $y = f(x + a)$ or $y = f(x - a)$.

questions.prompt: The turning point of $y = f(x)$ is $(2, -1)$. Where is the turning point of $y = -f(x) + 4$?
questions.solution: Work from the inside outwards. The reflection takes $(2, -1)$ to $(2, 1)$, then the $+4$ lifts it to $(2, 5)$. Adding first and reflecting second would give $(2, -3)$, so the order matters whenever a reflection is involved.

questions.prompt: The point $(4, 3)$ lies on $y = f(x)$. Which point lies on $y = f(x - 3) + 2$?
questions.solution: One change is inside and one is outside, so they act on different coordinates and the order does not matter. Inside moves $x$ right by $3$, giving $7$; outside lifts $y$ by $2$, giving $5$. The point is $(7, 5)$.

questions.prompt: Two graphs have turning points at $(2, -1)$ and $(2, 1)$, and the second curve opens downwards while the first opens upwards. What was the transformation?
questions.solution: The $x$ coordinate is unchanged and the height has flipped from $-1$ to $1$, and the curve has turned over. That is exactly $-f(x)$, a reflection in the $x$ axis. A translation $2$ up would lift the turning point to the same place but would leave the curve opening **upwards**, so the flip is what distinguishes them.

questions.prompt:
The curve $y = f(x)$ has $f(x) = x^2 - 4x + 3$, with roots at $x = 1$ and $x = 3$ and turning point $(2, -1)$.

(a) Describe fully the transformation from $y = f(x)$ to $y = f(x - 3)$, and give the new turning point and roots.

(b) Show by expanding that $f(x - 3) = x^2 - 10x + 24$, and check that your roots from part (a) are correct.
questions.solution: For part a, the change is inside the bracket, so it acts on x and the direction reverses: the minus three means the graph moves three to the right, not three to the left. So the transformation is a translation of three in the positive x direction. Since a horizontal translation leaves every height unchanged, the turning point keeps its y coordinate of minus one and its x coordinate increases by three, giving five, minus one. The roots move the same way, from one and three to four and six. For part b, substitute x minus three into f. That gives, bracket, x minus three, bracket, squared, minus four times, bracket, x minus three, bracket, plus three. Expanding the square gives x squared minus six x plus nine. Expanding the second term gives minus four x plus twelve. Adding the three, the whole thing is x squared minus six x plus nine minus four x plus twelve plus three. Collecting the x terms gives minus ten x, and collecting the constants gives nine plus twelve plus three, which is twenty four. So f of x minus three equals x squared minus ten x plus twenty four, as required. To check the roots, factorise: two numbers multiplying to twenty four and adding to minus ten are minus four and minus six, so it factorises to x minus four, times x minus six. The roots are therefore four and six, which is exactly what the translation predicted.

questions.prompt:
The point $P(4, 3)$ lies on the curve $y = f(x)$, whose turning point is $(2, -1)$.

(a) Give the coordinates of the image of $P$ on each of $y = f(x) + 2$, $y = f(x - 3)$, $y = -f(x)$ and $y = f(-x)$.

(b) One of these four transformations leaves the roots of the curve exactly where they were. Say which, and explain why.
questions.solution: For part a, take each in turn, remembering that only one coordinate ever changes. For y equals f of x plus two, the change is outside the bracket, so it affects the height only: the point becomes four, five. For y equals f of x minus three, the change is inside the bracket, so it affects x and reverses direction, moving three to the right: the point becomes seven, three. For y equals minus f of x, the minus is outside, so every height changes sign while x stays: the point becomes four, minus three. For y equals f of minus x, the minus is inside, so every x changes sign while the height stays: the point becomes minus four, three. For part b, the transformation that leaves the roots exactly where they were is y equals minus f of x, the reflection in the x axis. The reason is that a root is a point where the curve meets the x axis, which means its y coordinate is zero. Reflecting in the x axis replaces every y with minus y, and minus zero is zero, so a point already on the axis does not move at all. Every other point on the curve does move, which is why the curve turns upside down while its crossing points stay fixed. The reflection in the y axis, by contrast, moves the roots from one and three to minus one and minus three, and either translation moves them too.

examTechnique.body:
**Decide first whether the change is inside or outside the bracket.** That single question settles which axis moves and which direction.

- $f(x) + a$ — **up** by $a$. Outside, affects $y$, direction as written.
- $f(x + a)$ — **left** by $a$. Inside, affects $x$, direction reversed.
- $-f(x)$ — reflection in the **$x$ axis**. Outside, so the $y$ values flip.
- $f(-x)$ — reflection in the **$y$ axis**. Inside, so the $x$ values flip.

**Transform a point, not a curve.** If $(a, b)$ is on $y = f(x)$, then it is at $(a, b + 3)$ on $y = f(x) + 3$, at $(a + 3, b)$ on $y = f(x - 3)$, at $(a, -b)$ on $y = -f(x)$ and at $(-a, b)$ on $y = f(-x)$.

**Use the turning point as your anchor** when sketching. Move it by the rule, then draw the same shape around it.

**Say which transformation, and by how much.** "Translation by $\begin{pmatrix} 3 \\ 0 \end{pmatrix}$" or "translation $3$ to the right" both earn the mark; "it moves" does not. A reflection needs the **line** named: "reflection in the $x$ axis".

**Watch the sign in a given equation.** $y = f(x + 4)$ moves **left** $4$, because $x + 4$ is $x - (-4)$.

**A graph that is symmetrical can hide a transformation.** $y = x^2$ looks identical after $f(-x)$, which is why exam questions use a curve that is not symmetrical about the $y$ axis.
examinerErrors: Moving $f(x - 3)$ to the left instead of the right.
Reflecting $-f(x)$ in the $y$ axis rather than the $x$ axis.
Reflecting $f(-x)$ in the $x$ axis rather than the $y$ axis.
Changing both coordinates of a point when only one of them moves.
Saying "translation" without giving the direction or the distance.
Saying "reflection" without naming the line it is reflected in.
Testing a transformation on $y = x^2$, which is unchanged by $f(-x)$ and so proves nothing.
examTechnique.grade9Looks: A top answer asks one question first — is the change inside the bracket or outside it — and answers everything else from that. It transforms a named point rather than redrawing a curve, and uses the turning point as an anchor when a sketch is wanted. It describes a transformation completely: the kind, the direction and the distance for a translation, and the line for a reflection. It reads a plus inside the bracket as a move to the left without hesitating. And it never tests its understanding on a symmetrical curve, because a curve symmetrical about the y axis looks the same after f of minus x whether the rule was applied correctly or not.
